questions.question: Which of the following does not fall under the terms of credit?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Organizational hierarchy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Terms of credit** refer to the specific conditions that a lender and borrower agree upon for a loan or credit. These terms include factors such as **interest rates, repayment type, and recording requirements**, which are all essential for financial transactions and agreements.
 
• The **interest rate** is a crucial term of credit as it determines the cost of borrowing money. It indicates how much a borrower will pay over the principal amount for the duration of the loan. *Hence, this is correct and falls under the terms of credit.*
 
• **Repayment type** refers to the method or schedule of paying back the borrowed amount. Common repayment types include monthly installments or lump-sum payments, which define how the borrower fulfills their obligation. *This is also correct and part of the terms of credit.*
 
• **Recording requirements** involve maintaining clear documentation of the credit agreement, payments, and other related details. This ensures transparency and accountability in financial dealings. *This is also an essential part of the terms of credit.*
 
• **Organizational hierarchy**, however, refers to the structure or arrangement of authority and responsibility within an organization. It is unrelated to the financial terms agreed upon between a lender and borrower, making it irrelevant in the context of credit terms. *Hence, this is the correct answer as it does not fall under the terms of credit.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Key components of terms of credit:**

 
 
• **Interest rate:** It determines the cost of borrowing and is expressed as a percentage of the principal. For example, a 10% annual interest rate on a loan of Rs. 1,00,000 would incur an interest cost of Rs. 10,000 annually.
 
• **Collateral:** Some loans require collateral, which serves as security for the lender. If the borrower defaults, the lender can seize the collateral to recover the loan amount.
 
• **Repayment schedule:** This specifies the timing and frequency of payments, such as monthly installments or periodic bullet payments, ensuring clarity for both parties.
 
• **Loan tenure:** This is the duration for which the loan is granted. Short-term loans typically last for a few months to a year, while long-term loans may extend for decades.
 
 
 
• **Role of documentation in credit terms:**
 
 
• Proper documentation ensures the legality and enforceability of the credit agreement.
 
• It includes details such as the principal amount, interest rate, repayment schedule, and penalties for default.
 
 
 
• **Organizational hierarchy:**
 
 
• It is a structure that defines the roles and responsibilities of individuals within an organization.
 
• Examples include levels such as managers, team leaders, and employees, which dictate decision-making processes.
 
• Unlike credit terms, organizational hierarchy is relevant to management and operations rather than financial agreements.
 
 
 
• **Examples of credit terms in practice:**
 
 
• **Home loans:** Typically have long tenures (up to 30 years), fixed or floating interest rates, and monthly installment repayments.
 
• **Credit cards:** Offer short-term credit with high-interest rates, requiring minimum monthly payments to avoid penalties.
 
• **Business loans:** May involve variable interest rates, collateral requirements, and flexible repayment schedules tailored to business cash flow.

questions.question: Who among the following was the Minister of Home, Information and Broadcasting in the Interim Government formed in 1946?

__
 
• **Vallabhbhai Jhaverbhai Patel**, commonly known as Sardar Patel, was the **Minister of Home, Information and Broadcasting** in the **Interim Government of 1946**.
 
• The **Interim Government of India** was formed on **2nd September 1946** under the leadership of **Jawaharlal Nehru**.
 
• Sardar Patel played a crucial role in managing **internal security** and ensuring the smooth functioning of administrative machinery during a turbulent period before independence.
 
• As the Home Minister, Patel dealt with issues like **partition-related violence**, integration of princely states, and maintaining law and order.
 
• The **Information and Broadcasting portfolio** under Patel was important in communicating the policies of the Interim Government and fostering national unity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel:**

 
 
• Born on **31 October 1875**, in **Nadiad, Gujarat**, Patel was a prominent leader of the Indian freedom movement.
 
• He was instrumental in the **integration of more than 500 princely states** into the Union of India, earning him the title **"Iron Man of India."**
 
• Patel also served as the first **Deputy Prime Minister** and **Home Minister of independent India**.
 
• His efforts in nation-building are commemorated by the **Statue of Unity**, the world's tallest statue, located in Gujarat.
 
 
 
• **Interim Government of 1946:**
 
 
• It was a transitional government formed before India's independence on **15 August 1947**.
 
• The government was led by **Jawaharlal Nehru** as the Vice President of the Executive Council (equivalent to Prime Minister).
 
• It included members from both the **Indian National Congress** and the **Muslim League**, though the latter joined later.
 
• The Interim Government was responsible for framing policies and preparing the country for independence.

• **Dr. Rajendra Prasad:** Food and Agriculture Minister.
 
• **Abul Kalam Azad:** Education Minister.
 
• **Liaquat Ali Khan:** Finance Minister (from the Muslim League).
 
 
 
• **Challenges Faced by the Interim Government:**
 
 
• Handling **communal tensions** and violence during the partition of India.
 
• Negotiating with **British authorities** for the transfer of power.
 
• Dealing with the integration of **princely states** into the Indian Union.
 
• Establishing a framework for governance in independent India.

questions.question: Which of the following is a macronutrient present in soil?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Magnesium**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Magnesium** is classified as a macronutrient essential for plant growth and development. It is required in relatively large quantities compared to micronutrients like iron or zinc.
 
• Magnesium plays a critical role in the formation of **chlorophyll**, which is necessary for photosynthesis. This makes it vital for the plant's ability to produce energy.
 
• It acts as a central atom in the chlorophyll molecule, enabling the absorption of sunlight during the photosynthetic process.
 
• Magnesium also contributes to the activation of numerous enzymes involved in various metabolic processes in plants, including the synthesis of carbohydrates and proteins.
 
• Deficiency of magnesium in soil can result in symptoms such as **chlorosis** (yellowing of leaves), poor growth, and reduced yield in crops.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Macronutrients in Soil:**

 
 
• Macronutrients are elements that plants require in large amounts for their growth and development. These include **nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium, and sulfur.**
 
• Magnesium is considered one of the secondary macronutrients alongside calcium and sulfur, while nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium are primary macronutrients.
 
• It is typically absorbed by plants from the soil in the form of **Mg2+ ions.**
 
 
 
• **Micronutrients in Soil:**
 
 
• Micronutrients, also known as trace elements, are nutrients required by plants in smaller quantities. Examples include **iron, zinc, manganese, copper, molybdenum, boron, and chlorine.**
 
• Though required in small amounts, micronutrients are vital for plant biochemical processes like enzyme activation and hormone synthesis.
 
 
 
• **Functions of Magnesium:**
 
 
• **Photosynthesis:** Magnesium is the central atom in chlorophyll, allowing plants to capture light energy.
 
• **Enzyme Activation:** It activates enzymes responsible for the synthesis of DNA, RNA, and other cellular components.
 
• **Nutrient Transport:** Magnesium aids in the transport of nutrients within the plant, ensuring proper growth and metabolic function.
 
 
 
• **Symptoms of Magnesium Deficiency:**
 
 
• **Chlorosis:** Yellowing of leaves due to insufficient chlorophyll production.
 
• **Leaf Curling:** Margins of leaves may curl upwards or downwards.
 
• **Stunted Growth:** Plants may exhibit slow growth and lower productivity.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Magnesium-Rich Fertilizers:**
 
 
• **Dolomite Lime:** Used to add magnesium and calcium to soil.
 
• **Epsom Salt:** Commonly used as a quick source of magnesium in agriculture.

questions.question: Which of the following types of agriculture depends on monsoon and natural fertility of the soil?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ancient subsistence farming**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Ancient subsistence farming** is a traditional form of agriculture that relies heavily on **monsoons** and the **natural fertility of the soil** to produce crops for local consumption.
 
• This farming method is primarily practiced in regions where farmers rely on **rain-fed irrigation** systems due to the lack of modern irrigation facilities.
 
• It is characterized by the use of **basic tools** and **traditional techniques**, with minimal or no use of modern machinery or chemical fertilizers.
 
• Farmers focus on cultivating crops like **rice, wheat, maize, and pulses**, which are essential for their subsistence and local food security.
 
• Ancient subsistence farming is still practiced in many rural areas of developing countries, including **India, parts of Africa, and Southeast Asia**, where modern agricultural advancements have not fully penetrated.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Intensive subsistence farming:**

 
 
• This type of farming is practiced in regions with a high population density, like **India, China, and Southeast Asia**.
 
• It involves the cultivation of small landholdings with intensive use of labor and inputs like chemical fertilizers to maximize crop yield.
 
• Crops like **rice, wheat, and millets** are commonly grown under this system, with an emphasis on meeting the food needs of the family and the local market.
 
 
 
• **Plantation farming:**
 
 
• Plantation farming is a type of commercial agriculture where crops are grown on a large scale for export purposes.
 
• Crops like **tea, coffee, rubber, and sugarcane** are cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions like **India, Brazil, and Malaysia**.
 
• This method relies on modern machinery, skilled labor, and significant capital investment, unlike subsistence farming.
 
 
 
• **Commercial farming:**
 
 
• This method focuses on growing crops and raising livestock for sale in the market rather than for personal consumption.
 
• It is characterized by the use of modern technology, hybrid seeds, and chemical inputs to achieve high productivity.
 
• Commercial farming is common in developed nations like the **USA, Canada, and parts of Europe**.
 
 
 
• **Natural factors influencing subsistence farming:**
 
 
• Subsistence farming is heavily dependent on **natural factors** such as rainfall, soil fertility, and seasonal climatic conditions.
 
• Regions with a **monsoon-dependent climate** like India and Southeast Asia are conducive to this type of farming.
 
• The lack of advanced irrigation facilities often makes farmers vulnerable to **droughts and floods**.
 
 
 
• [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points**__
 
 
• **Monsoons:** Monsoons are a significant factor for regions practicing subsistence farming. They provide the **necessary water supply** for crops, especially in rain-fed areas.
 
• **Soil fertility:** Natural soil fertility plays a crucial role as chemical fertilizers are rarely used in subsistence farming.
 
• **Tools and techniques:** Farmers rely on **traditional tools** like plows, sickles, and hoes, and use age-old farming techniques passed down through generations.

questions.question: Evidence of cultivation of coarse grains in ancient India has been found at which of the following sites?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Hallur**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Hallur**, located in the Dharwad district of Karnataka, is one of the earliest sites in South India where evidence of agricultural practices, including the cultivation of coarse grains, has been discovered.
 
• Archaeological excavations at Hallur have revealed the presence of **millets** such as ragi (finger millet) and jowar (sorghum), indicating that these grains were part of the diet in ancient India.
 
• Hallur is associated with the **Neolithic culture** and provides crucial evidence of early agricultural practices, animal domestication, and settled life in South India.
 
• The findings at Hallur date back to approximately 2000 BCE, signifying one of the earliest instances of settled agricultural activity in peninsular India.
 
• The site also provides evidence of **pottery** and tools, which further highlight the Neolithic lifestyle and the advances made by the people in this region during that period.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Gufkral**:

 
 
• Located in the **Kashmir Valley**, Gufkral is a Neolithic site that provides evidence of early agricultural practices.
 
• Excavations at Gufkral have revealed the cultivation of wheat and barley, along with the domestication of sheep and goats.
 
• The site also features pit dwellings, tools, and pottery, highlighting the early transition to a settled life in northern India.
 
 
 
• **Koldihwa**:
 
 
• Koldihwa is a Neolithic site located in present-day Uttar Pradesh.
 
• It is known for providing evidence of the cultivation of rice, one of the earliest examples of rice agriculture in India.
 
• The site also contains remnants of pottery, microlithic tools, and evidence of cattle domestication.
 
 
 
• **Chirand**:
 
 
• Chirand is an important archaeological site in Bihar, dating back to the **Neolithic period**.
 
• Findings from Chirand include evidence of wheat, barley, and rice cultivation, along with animal domestication.
 
• The site is also notable for its terracotta figurines, beads, and pottery.
 
 
 
• **Coarse grains in ancient India**:
 
 
• Coarse grains such as millets (ragi, jowar, and bajra) played a crucial role in the diet of ancient Indians due to their adaptability to arid regions.
 
• These grains are rich in **nutrients**, including iron, calcium, and fiber, and were cultivated extensively in regions with limited water resources.
 
• They are still an integral part of Indian agriculture and diet, particularly in regions like Karnataka, Rajasthan, and Maharashtra.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The cultivation of coarse grains like millets is significant as it marks the beginning of agricultural practices in India.
 
• The Neolithic period, which began around 7000 BCE in India, is characterized by the advent of agriculture, animal domestication, and the use of polished stone tools.
 
• Sites like Hallur, Koldihwa, and Chirand provide valuable insights into the agricultural and cultural practices of early Indian communities.
 
• Millets, being highly drought-resistant, were suitable for the semi-arid regions of the Indian subcontinent and played a vital role in sustaining early civilizations.

questions.question: According to the Indian Constitution, the use of English language for official work was discontinued in which of the following years?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1965**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Indian Constitution** originally provided for the use of both **English** and **Hindi** for official purposes of the Union government for a period of **15 years** from the commencement of the Constitution (i.e., till 26 January 1965).
 
• However, due to opposition from non-Hindi-speaking states, particularly in **South India**, the Parliament enacted the **Official Languages Act, 1963**.
 
• This Act allowed the continued use of the **English language** for official purposes even after 1965, alongside Hindi, as long as the non-Hindi-speaking states demanded it.
 
• The year **1965** marked the end of the Constitutionally mandated use of English for official purposes, but it did not completely discontinue it due to the provisions of the **Official Languages Act, 1963**.
 
• Thus, the use of English was constitutionally discontinued as a **mandatory provision** in **1965**, though practically, it continued to be used along with Hindi.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Official Language Provisions in the Constitution:**

 
 
• **Article 343**: Declares Hindi in the **Devanagari script** as the official language of the Union.
 
• **Article 344**: Provides for the constitution of a **Commission and Parliamentary Committee** to recommend the progressive use of Hindi for official purposes.
 
• **Schedule VIII**: Lists 22 languages recognized by the Constitution, including Hindi and English.
 
 
 
• **Official Languages Act, 1963:**
 
 
• Enacted to address the concerns of non-Hindi-speaking regions regarding the continued use of English after 1965.
 
• Permitted the use of English for official purposes of the Union and for communication between the Union and non-Hindi-speaking states.
 
 
 
• **Anti-Hindi Agitation:**
 
 
• The **1965 Anti-Hindi Agitation** in Tamil Nadu was a major protest against the mandatory imposition of Hindi as the sole official language.
 
• It led to the assurance by the government that English would continue to be used alongside Hindi for official purposes.
 
 
 
• **Present Scenario:**

questions.question: Which of the following types of soil is formed in areas with high temperature and heavy rainfall?

__
 
• **Laterite soil** is formed in areas with **high temperature and heavy rainfall**, which lead to intense leaching of soil minerals.
 
• This type of soil is characterized by its **red to reddish-brown color**, due to the high content of iron oxides.
 
• The soil develops in tropical and subtropical regions, particularly in areas of India such as **Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Odisha, and Maharashtra**.
 
• Due to heavy rainfall, soluble minerals like silica are leached away, leaving behind oxides of iron and aluminum, which are insoluble and accumulate in the soil.
 
• It is generally poor in fertility and lacks essential nutrients like **nitrogen, potassium, and lime**, but it can be made productive with proper fertilizers and irrigation.

• **Characteristics of Laterite Soil:**

 
 
• It contains a high concentration of **iron oxide and aluminum**, giving it a reddish appearance.
 
• Laterite soil is formed through the process of **laterization**, where heavy rains wash away silica, leaving behind oxides of iron and aluminum.
 
• It is acidic in nature and has poor organic matter content, which reduces its suitability for most crops unless supplemented with fertilizers.
 
• It hardens irreversibly when exposed to air, which makes it useful for making bricks and construction material.
 
 
 
• **Distribution of Laterite Soil:**
 
 
• In India, laterite soil is found in states like **Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Odisha, Assam, and parts of Chhattisgarh**.
 
• Globally, laterite soils are common in **tropical and subtropical regions**, such as parts of Africa, South America, and Southeast Asia.
 
 
 
• **Uses of Laterite Soil:**
 
 
• It is used for growing crops like **cashew nuts, coffee, tea, and rubber**, with proper soil management.
 
• Laterite soil is also widely used as a raw material in the **construction industry** due to its ability to harden upon exposure to air.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Soils:**
 
 
• **Dry soil:** Found in arid regions, it has low water retention and supports xerophytic vegetation. It lacks the leaching process seen in laterite soil.
 
• **Red soil:** Found in regions with moderate rainfall, it is rich in iron but less leached compared to laterite soil.
 
• **Black soil:** Known for its water retention capacity, it is formed in regions with low rainfall and is ideal for cotton cultivation.

__
 
• **Bahadur Shah Zafar**, the last Mughal emperor, was the ruler of India during the **Revolt of 1857**, also known as the First War of Indian Independence.
 
• He was a symbolic leader of the revolt as Indian soldiers and citizens saw him as a unifying figure against British colonial rule.
 
• The **Revolt of 1857** began as a mutiny by sepoys in the British East India Company’s army but quickly spread across northern and central India. It was one of the largest uprisings against British rule.
 
• Bahadur Shah Zafar, though aged and lacking actual military power, was proclaimed the emperor by the rebels, giving the movement legitimacy and symbolic strength.
 
• After the revolt was suppressed by the British, Bahadur Shah Zafar was captured, tried, and exiled to **Rangoon (present-day Yangon, Myanmar)**, where he died in 1862.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bahadur Shah Zafar:**

 
 
• Born in **1775**, he was the last Mughal emperor, ascending the throne in **1837**.
 
• His rule was largely symbolic as the British East India Company controlled most of India, reducing him to a figurehead with limited authority confined to Delhi.
 
• He was an accomplished poet and is remembered for his Urdu poetry, which reflects themes of love, loss, and patriotism.
 
 
 
• **The Revolt of 1857:**
 
 
• This was the first large-scale uprising against British colonial rule in India, often referred to as the **First War of Independence**.
 
• The revolt started on **10 May 1857**, when sepoys (Indian soldiers in the British army) in Meerut rebelled against their officers, triggered by the use of greased cartridges believed to be laced with cow and pig fat.
 
• The revolt spread to major cities like Delhi, Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi, and Gwalior.
 
• Although the revolt was ultimately suppressed, it marked the beginning of Indian nationalism and sowed the seeds for future independence movements.
 
 
 
• **Aftermath of the Revolt:**
 
 
• Following the revolt, the British government dissolved the East India Company and took direct control over India in **1858**.
 
• The policy of annexation under the Doctrine of Lapse was abandoned, and efforts were made to win the loyalty of Indian princes and elites.
 
• The British reorganized the army, placing greater emphasis on loyalty and minimizing the number of Indian soldiers in the ranks.
 
 
 
• **Other Mughal Emperors (Incorrect Options):**
 
 
• **Shah Jahan:** Known for building the Taj Mahal, he ruled from **1628 to 1658** and was not involved in the revolt of 1857.
 
• **Aurangzeb:** A powerful Mughal ruler who expanded the empire significantly, he ruled from **1658 to 1707**, long before the revolt.
 
• **Jahangir:** The fourth Mughal emperor, he ruled from **1605 to 1627**, known for his love of art and culture but not connected to the revolt of 1857.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• The revolt marked the end of the Mughal Empire, as the British formally abolished it after exiling Bahadur Shah Zafar.
 
• It had significant social, political, and economic impacts, leading to changes in British policies in India.

• **Mohiniyattam** is a classical dance form from the state of **Kerala**, India.
 
• This dance form combines elements of **Bharatanatyam** and **Kathakali**, showcasing grace and elegance in its movements.
 
• Mohiniyattam is traditionally performed by **women** and is known for its **Lasya style** (feminine and graceful movements).

• **Kalhana**, a renowned 12th-century Sanskrit poet and historian, authored the **Rajatarangini**, a historical chronicle of the kings of **Kashmir**.
 
• The **Rajatarangini**, meaning "River of Kings," is considered the most authentic historical record of ancient Kashmir and provides a detailed account of its rulers from ancient times to the 12th century CE.
 
• Kalhana's work is known for its literary richness and historical depth. It combines historical events with poetic elegance, offering a unique blend of history and literature.
 
• The text is divided into **eight books (Tarangas)**, each chronicling a specific period in Kashmir's history, starting from the mythical origins of its rulers to Kalhana's contemporary times.
 
• The **Rajatarangini** remains a vital source of information for historians studying the socio-political, cultural, and religious aspects of ancient Kashmir.

• Kalhana adopted a critical approach to historical writing. He cross-verified sources and criticized the actions of rulers, ensuring a relatively unbiased narrative.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of Kashmir's History in Rajatarangini**:
 
 
• Kashmir's rulers were described as patrons of art, architecture, and literature. The region was a cultural hub during ancient times.

• It records significant events such as invasions, internal strife, and socio-political changes in the region.

• **Rajasthan**: Rajasthan's history revolves around the Rajput dynasties, including the Mewar and Marwar kingdoms. Kalhana's Rajatarangini focuses exclusively on Kashmir, not Rajasthan.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Rajatarangini**:
 
 
• It provides detailed insights into the administration, society, and culture of ancient Kashmir.
 
• The text is a valuable resource for understanding the interplay between politics and religion in medieval India.
 
• Historians often refer to it for reconstructing the history of Kashmir and its rulers.

questions.question: Why does the Government of India declare the minimum support price of crops before the sowing season begins?

options.text: To provide them with money for seeds
To provide protection to farmers from price volatility
To provide them with funds for irrigation

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To provide protection to farmers from price volatility**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Minimum Support Price (MSP)** is declared by the **Government of India** before the sowing season to ensure that farmers are protected against unpredictable price fluctuations in the market.
 
• The primary objective of MSP is to **safeguard farmers** by guaranteeing a minimum price for their produce, irrespective of market conditions, thereby reducing the risk of loss.
 
• It helps in providing a sense of **financial security** to farmers, encouraging them to grow crops without fear of incurring heavy losses due to price crashes during harvest time.
 
• The MSP is determined by the **Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP)**, which considers factors such as the cost of production, demand and supply, and market trends.
 
• This policy has proven to be particularly beneficial in addressing the issue of **price volatility**, which is caused by factors such as unpredictable weather, market dynamics, and global influences on agricultural commodities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **What is Minimum Support Price (MSP)?**

 
 
• MSP is the price at which the government purchases crops directly from the farmer, regardless of the market price.
 
• It is announced for **22 crops** including rice, wheat, pulses, and oilseeds as per the recommendations of the **CACP**.
 
• The policy ensures that farmers are not compelled to sell their produce at distress prices.
 
 
 
• **Role of MSP in Agriculture:**
 
 
• It provides a **guaranteed market** for farmers' produce, thereby reducing the risk of losses during harvest seasons.
 
• Encourages farmers to grow staple crops like wheat and rice, ensuring food security in the country.
 
• Helps stabilize agricultural incomes and supports rural livelihoods.
 
 
 
• **Price Volatility in Agriculture:**
 
 
• Price volatility refers to **unpredictable fluctuations** in crop prices due to factors such as weather conditions, pests, and global market trends.
 
• It negatively impacts small and marginal farmers, making them financially vulnerable.
 
 
 
• **Other Benefits of MSP:**
 
 
• Encourages farmers to adopt modern agricultural techniques by ensuring financial returns.
 
• Promotes the cultivation of certain crops, contributing to the balanced development of agriculture.
 
• Supports the Public Distribution System (PDS) as the government procures food grains at MSP for redistribution to economically weaker sections.
 
 
 
• [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 
• The **Agricultural Price Policy**, including MSP, was introduced in **1965** to tackle the food crisis and ensure fair returns to farmers.
 
• In India, MSP is particularly significant for crops such as wheat, rice, sugarcane, and cotton, which are widely cultivated.
 
• The government also uses MSP as a tool to encourage the production of certain crops and ensure a balanced agricultural economy.

• The map provided an extensive survey of the Indian subcontinent, marking important towns, rivers, and geographical features.

• Born in **1742** in England, Rennell was a geographer, historian, and cartographer.
 
• He was appointed as the **Surveyor General of Bengal** at the age of 21.
 
• His most famous works include the *A Bengal Atlas* and *Memoir of a Map of Hindoostan*.

questions.question: Which of the following techniques was used to make stone tools in ancient India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pressure Flaking**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Pressure Flaking** is a technique used in ancient tool-making where a sharp instrument, such as a bone, antler, or wood, is used to apply pressure to the edge of a stone core to remove small flakes and shape the tool.
 
• This method was used to create sharp edges and refine tools like arrowheads, spearheads, and knives, making them more efficient and precise for hunting or cutting.
 
• **Pressure Flaking** was a significant advancement compared to earlier methods like direct percussion, as it allowed for greater control over the size and shape of the flakes removed.
 
• It was particularly prominent during the **Mesolithic and Neolithic periods**, where more sophisticated tools were needed for activities such as farming and hunting.
 
• The tools created using this method were generally smaller and sharper than those made using older techniques, reflecting the evolution of human craftsmanship and technological skills.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Step Flaking:**

 
 
• This technique involves striking the stone at specific angles to create a "step" pattern. It was primarily used in the Paleolithic period to create larger, less refined tools.
 
• Step flaking often resulted in uneven surfaces and was less precise compared to pressure flaking.
 
 
 
• **Bipolar Technique:**
 
 
• In this method, a stone core is placed on a hard surface and struck from above, causing it to split. It was used to create smaller flakes and tools.
 
• This technique is often associated with the production of microliths in later prehistoric periods.
 
 
 
• **Pecking:**
 
 
• Pecking involves striking a stone repeatedly with a harder stone to shape it. This technique was used to create larger tools, such as axes and hammers.
 
• It was more common in the Neolithic period when polished tools became essential for activities like agriculture.
 
 
 
• **Evolution of Stone Tool Technologies:**
 
 
• Stone tool-making techniques evolved from basic percussion methods in the Paleolithic era to more refined methods like pressure flaking in the Mesolithic and Neolithic periods.
 
• This evolution reflects the increasing complexity of human societies and their need for specialized tools to meet different challenges.
 
 
 
• [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 
• **Pressure Flaking** was essential for creating tools with fine edges required for specific tasks, such as cutting, scraping, or drilling.
 
• This technique highlights the ingenuity of early humans and their ability to innovate with available resources, marking a major step in the development of human technology.
 
• Archaeological evidence of pressure flaking has been found in regions such as Africa, Europe, and India, showcasing its widespread use.

questions.question: Which of the following subjects is part of the State List of the Government of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Agriculture**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Agriculture** is a subject listed under the **State List** as per the **Seventh Schedule** of the **Indian Constitution**.
 
• The **State List** comprises subjects where the state legislatures have the exclusive power to make laws, as provided in **Article 246** of the Constitution.
 
• Agriculture includes activities such as **farming, irrigation, land improvement, land tenure, and agricultural education**, which are under the jurisdiction of individual states.
 
• This decentralization allows each state to address its unique agricultural needs and challenges, given the vast diversity in soil, climate, and resources across the country.
 
• The inclusion of agriculture in the State List ensures that states have the authority to implement **policies, schemes, and subsidies** to benefit farmers within their respective territories.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **State List under the Seventh Schedule:**

 
 
• The Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution divides legislative powers between the **Union List, State List, and Concurrent List**.
 
• The State List includes **61 subjects** (originally 66), such as **public health, police, local government, and agriculture**.
 
• States have exclusive powers to legislate on subjects in the State List, enabling decentralization and regional autonomy.
 
 
 
• **Other Lists under the Seventh Schedule:**
 
 
• **Union List:** Comprises **97 subjects** (originally 100) such as defense, foreign affairs, banking, and telecommunications. The Parliament has exclusive power to legislate on these subjects.
 
• **Concurrent List:** Includes **52 subjects** (originally 47) like education, forests, and marriage. Both the Parliament and state legislatures can make laws on these subjects, but in case of conflict, Union law prevails.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Agriculture in India:**
 
 
• Agriculture is the primary source of livelihood for about **58% of India's population**, contributing around **18-20% to the GDP**.
 
• India is the world's largest producer of **spices, pulses, milk, tea, and jute**, and the second-largest producer of **wheat, rice, fruits, and vegetables**.
 
• Major agricultural schemes include **PM-Kisan, PMFBY (Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana), and eNAM (National Agriculture Market)** to support farmers.
 
 
 
• **Characteristics of the Other Options:**
 
 
• **Banking:** Falls under the **Union List**, as it is a matter of national importance and is regulated by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI).
 
• **Succession:** Listed in the **Concurrent List**, allowing both the Union and state governments to legislate on matters related to inheritance and succession.
 
• **Marriage:** Also part of the **Concurrent List**, with laws like the **Special Marriage Act** and **Hindu Marriage Act** governed jointly by both Union and state governments.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The distribution of powers between the Union and states is a key feature of **federalism** in India, ensuring governance at both central and regional levels.
 
• The **State List** empowers states to focus on issues specific to their region, fostering localized solutions and governance.
 
• Any conflict regarding legislative competence is resolved by the judiciary, ensuring adherence to the **Constitutional framework**.

questions.question: On which portion of the human eye is the image formed?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Retina**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **retina** is a thin layer of tissue located at the back of the human eye, responsible for capturing light and forming images.
 
• When light enters the eye, it passes through the **cornea, pupil, and lens** to reach the retina, where an image is formed.
 
• The retina contains two types of photoreceptor cells: **rods** and **cones**. Rods are responsible for vision in dim light, while cones allow for color perception and function best in bright light.
 
• The image formed on the retina is **inverted and real**. The brain processes and interprets this image to provide correct orientation and meaningful vision.
 
• The retina plays a crucial role in converting light signals into **electrical signals**, which are transmitted to the brain through the optic nerve for visual interpretation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Iris:**

 
 
• The iris is the colored part of the eye that controls the size of the pupil, regulating the amount of light entering the eye.
 
• It does not play a direct role in image formation but helps adjust light intensity for better vision.
 
 
 
• **Cornea:**
 
 
• The cornea is the transparent, dome-shaped front layer of the eye that focuses incoming light onto the lens.
 
• It provides most of the eye's refractive power but does not form the final image.
 
 
 
• **Pupil:**
 
 
• The pupil is the dark circular opening in the center of the iris that allows light to enter the eye.
 
• It adjusts its size based on light intensity but does not contribute to image formation.
 
 
 
• **Optic Nerve:**
 
 
• The optic nerve carries visual information from the retina to the brain.
 
• It plays a crucial role in processing and interpreting visual signals but is not involved in the physical formation of the image.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• The retina is part of the **central nervous system** and is essential for vision.
 
• Conditions like **retinal detachment** or **macular degeneration** can severely affect vision.
 
• The retina's functionality is supported by other eye structures like the cornea, lens, and vitreous humor.
 
• Regular eye check-ups are crucial to monitor retinal health and detect any potential issues early.

• This act was formulated by **Dietrich Brandis**, a German expert, who is considered the father of Indian forestry.
 
• The act primarily aimed to establish the British government’s control over forests and to ensure a continuous supply of timber, especially for railway sleepers.
 
• It granted the government the right to declare forests as state property and restrict the use of forest resources by local communities.
 
• Although the 1865 act laid the foundation, it underwent significant amendments in subsequent years, particularly in **1878** and **1927**, to strengthen forest management and conservation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Dietrich Brandis:**

 
 
• He was a **German botanist** and forester who is regarded as the founder of scientific forestry in India.
 
• Brandis served as the first Inspector General of Forests in India, a position he held from **1864 to 1883**.
 
• He introduced methods of systematic forest management and emphasized the need for sustainable use of resources.
 
• Brandis also established the **Imperial Forest School** at Dehradun in 1878 to train forest officers.
 
 
 
• **Indian Forest Act, 1878:**
 
 
• This act replaced the 1865 act and classified forests into three categories: **reserved forests, protected forests, and village forests**.
 
• It imposed stricter regulations on the use of forest resources by local communities.
 
• The act marked a significant step towards centralizing forest administration under British control.
 
 
 
• **Indian Forest Act, 1927:**
 
 
• This act consolidated previous legislation and remains the cornerstone of forest management in India to this day.
 
• It provided a legal framework for the protection and management of forests and wildlife.
 
• The act also defined offenses such as illegal felling of trees, hunting, and encroachment on forest land.
 
 
 
• **Forest Conservation in India:**
 
 
• Post-independence, the focus on forest conservation gained momentum with the enactment of the **Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980**.
 
• India’s forest policies now emphasize both conservation and sustainable development while recognizing the rights of forest-dependent communities.
 
• Initiatives such as the **Joint Forest Management (JFM)** program involve local communities in forest conservation efforts.

questions.question: Which of the following classical dances received a revival due to the Mughal influence on Indian culture?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kathak**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Kathak** is one of the eight classical dance forms of India that traces its origins to storytelling traditions in North India.
 
• During the **Mughal era**, Kathak underwent a significant transformation, incorporating Persian influences such as intricate footwork, rhythmic patterns, and flowing costumes. Hence, it received revival due to Mughal influence.
 
• The Mughal rulers promoted Kathak as a court dance, emphasizing its aesthetic appeal and introducing Persian poetry and music into its performances. 
 
• Kathak later evolved into two distinct styles: the **Lucknow Gharana**, known for its graceful expressions, and the **Jaipur Gharana**, which highlighted footwork and rhythm. 
 
• As a result of the Mughal patronage, Kathak transitioned from a devotional dance performed in temples to a refined art form popular in royal courts. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Odissi:**

 
 
• Originated in **Odisha**, it is one of the oldest classical dance forms in India.
 
• Odissi is primarily performed as a form of devotion to Lord Jagannath and is deeply rooted in temple rituals. 
 
• This dance form is characterized by its **graceful movements**, sculpturesque poses, and intricate footwork.
 
• It was revived during the **20th century** by modern practitioners, but it did not receive any significant influence from Mughal culture.
 
 
 
• **Kuchipudi:**
 
 
• Kuchipudi originated in **Andhra Pradesh** and is both a dance and drama form.
 
• It is deeply associated with **Vaishnavism** and often portrays stories from Hindu epics like the Mahabharata and Ramayana. 
 
• The dance form involves intricate rhythms, expressions, and dramatic storytelling but lacks Persian or Mughal influence.
 
 
 
• **Kathakali:**
 
 
• Kathakali is a classical dance drama that originated in **Kerala**.
 
• Known for its elaborate costumes, makeup, and exaggerated expressions, Kathakali depicts stories from Hindu epics like the Ramayana and Mahabharata.
 
• It is a temple art form and remained untouched by Mughal cultural influences.
 
 
 
• **Classical Dance Forms of India:**
 
 
• India has **eight recognized classical dance forms**: Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kathakali, Kuchipudi, Odissi, Manipuri, Mohiniyattam, and Sattriya.
 
• Each classical dance form reflects the cultural heritage, religious traditions, and artistic practices of its region of origin.
 
 
 
• [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 
• **Kathak** was influenced by Persian, Central Asian, and Mughal cultural elements during its evolution, making it distinct among the classical dances of India.
 
• Mughal patronage led to the incorporation of Persian poetry, music, and attire into Kathak, transforming it into a court dance.

questions.question: Citizenship is described in which of the following parts of the Indian Constitution?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Part II**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Part II** of the **Indian Constitution** deals with the provisions related to **citizenship** in India.
 
• This part includes **Articles 5 to 11**, which define various aspects of citizenship, such as who is a citizen of India at the commencement of the Constitution, acquisition, and termination of citizenship.
 
• **Article 5** specifies citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution for people domiciled in India.
 
• **Article 6** provides for citizenship rights for persons who migrated to India from Pakistan before or after the partition.
 
• **Article 9** states that any person voluntarily acquiring citizenship of a foreign state will cease to be an Indian citizen.
 
• **Article 11** empowers the Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law, allowing it to make laws regarding the acquisition and termination of citizenship.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Acquisition of Citizenship**:

 
 
• The Citizenship Act, 1955, governs the acquisition and termination of Indian citizenship. It provides for citizenship by **birth, descent, registration, naturalization, and incorporation of territory**.
 
• Citizenship by birth applies to individuals born in India after January 26, 1950, and before July 1, 1987, or if one of the parents is an Indian citizen after this date.
 
• Citizenship by descent applies to individuals born outside India to an Indian parent.
 
 
 
• **Termination of Citizenship**:
 
 
• Indian citizenship can be terminated by **renunciation, deprivation, or acquisition of foreign citizenship.**
 
• Renunciation is a voluntary act by which a person gives up their Indian citizenship.
 
• Deprivation is a compulsory termination by the Government of India for reasons such as fraud during the acquisition of citizenship.
 
 
 
• **Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI):**
 
 
• The Government of India offers an OCI card to individuals of Indian origin who are citizens of other countries, allowing them certain rights in India, excluding voting and holding constitutional offices.
 
 
 
• **Important Amendments:**
 
 
• The **Citizenship Amendment Act, 2019** allows citizenship for persecuted religious minorities from Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan, specifically Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis, and Christians.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Fundamental Rights and Citizenship:**

 
 
• Only Indian citizens enjoy certain fundamental rights, such as the right to equality of opportunity in public employment (Article 16) and the right to vote in elections.
 
 
 
• **Dual Citizenship:**
 
 
• India does not allow dual citizenship, meaning an Indian citizen cannot simultaneously hold citizenship of another country.
 
 
 
• **Role of Parliament:**
 
 
• Under Article 11, Parliament has the authority to create laws governing citizenship, including acquisition, renunciation, and termination.

questions.question: Which of the following mountain peaks is located in Nepal?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Dhaulagiri**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Dhaulagiri** is a mountain peak located in the **Himalayan range of Nepal**. It is the **seventh highest mountain in the world**, with an elevation of **8,167 meters (26,795 feet)**.
 
• The peak lies in the **Dhaulagiri massif**, which is separated from the Annapurna range by the **Kali Gandaki Gorge**, one of the deepest gorges in the world.
 
• **Dhaulagiri I**, the main peak of the massif, was first successfully climbed on **May 13, 1960**, by a Swiss/Austrian expedition.
 
• The name "Dhaulagiri" is derived from the Sanskrit words **"Dhawala"** (meaning dazzling, white, or beautiful) and **"Giri"** (meaning mountain).
 
• Being part of Nepal's Himalayan range, Dhaulagiri is a vital component of the country's tourism and adventure trekking industry.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Kanchenjunga:**

 
 
• **Kanchenjunga** is the **third highest mountain in the world**, with an elevation of **8,586 meters (28,169 feet)**. It is located in the **eastern Himalayas**, straddling the border between **Nepal and India**.
 
• The mountain has **five peaks**, and its name translates to "**Five Treasures of Snow**" in Tibetan.
 
• Kanchenjunga is a prominent peak for mountaineering and trekking, attracting climbers globally.
 
 
 
• **Kamet:**
 
 
• **Kamet** is the **second highest mountain in the Garhwal region** of Uttarakhand, India, with an elevation of **7,756 meters (25,446 feet)**.
 
• It is part of the **Indian Himalayan range** and is located near the Tibetan Plateau.
 
• Kamet's remote location makes it less accessible compared to other peaks in the region.
 
 
 
• **Nanda Devi:**
 
 
• **Nanda Devi** is the **highest mountain located entirely within India**, with an elevation of **7,816 meters (25,643 feet)**.
 
• It is part of the **Garhwal Himalayas**, situated in Uttarakhand, and is known for its stunning beauty and rich biodiversity.
 
• The **Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve** surrounding the peak is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Nepal's Himalayan Peaks:**
 
 
• Nepal is home to **eight of the world's fourteen peaks** above 8,000 meters, including **Mount Everest**, the highest peak globally.
 
• The Himalayan range is a hub for **mountaineering, trekking, and adventure tourism**, contributing significantly to Nepal's economy.
 
• The mountains are also vital for the region's **ecosystem and biodiversity**, providing water resources and supporting flora and fauna.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Geographical Significance:**

 
 
• The Himalayan range, including peaks like Dhaulagiri, plays a crucial role in shaping the **climate and weather patterns** of South Asia.
 
• The mountains act as a barrier to the monsoon winds, leading to heavy rainfall in the region.
 
• The range is also a source of **major rivers** such as the Ganges, Brahmaputra, and Indus.
 
 
 
• **Tourism and Economy:**
 
 
• Nepal's Himalayan peaks are a major attraction for **adventure tourism**, including trekking, climbing, and expeditions.
 
• Tourism related to the Himalayas contributes significantly to Nepal's **GDP** and provides livelihoods to local communities.

__
 
• **Sonam Lochar** is one of the most significant festivals celebrated in **Sikkim**. It is observed by the **Bhutia** and **Lepcha communities**, who follow the **Buddhist tradition**.
 
• This festival marks the **new year** as per the **Tibetan Lunar Calendar** and is celebrated with great enthusiasm, including rituals, dances, and community feasts.
 
• **Monasteries** in Sikkim, such as the **Rumtek Monastery**, become centers of celebration during this festival. Monks perform traditional dances like the **Cham Dance** to ward off evil spirits.
 
• The festival generally falls in the months of **January or February**, depending on the Lunar Calendar. It is marked by prayers, cultural performances, and traditional food.
 
• *Hence, the correct answer is Sonam Lochar.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

questions.question: The green coloured plastids in a plant cell are known as:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**chloroplasts**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Chloroplasts** are the **green-coloured plastids** in plant cells responsible for the process of **photosynthesis**, which converts light energy into chemical energy.
 
• These organelles contain the pigment **chlorophyll**, which is essential for capturing light energy from the sun.
 
• Chloroplasts are **double-membrane-bound organelles** and are primarily found in the green tissues of plants, such as leaves.
 
• The internal structure of chloroplasts includes **thylakoids, grana, and stroma**. Thylakoids are flattened sac-like membranes, while grana are stacks of thylakoids where light-dependent reactions occur.
 
• Chloroplasts are unique to plants and some algae, making them vital for sustaining life on Earth by producing **oxygen** and organic compounds.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Chloroplast Structure:**

 
 
• **Outer membrane:** The smooth outer boundary of the chloroplast that is permeable to small molecules.
 
• **Inner membrane:** It regulates the passage of materials in and out of the chloroplast and contains enzymes essential for metabolic functions.
 
• **Thylakoid membrane:** Contains chlorophyll and is the site of the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis.
 
• **Stroma:** The fluid-filled space inside chloroplasts where the Calvin cycle (light-independent reactions) occurs, producing glucose.
 
 
 
• **Chlorophyll:**
 
 
• Chlorophyll is the primary pigment in chloroplasts, responsible for the green colour of plants.
 
• There are different types of chlorophyll, such as **chlorophyll a** and **chlorophyll b**, which absorb light in the blue and red wavelengths while reflecting green light.
 
 
 
• **Functions of Chloroplasts:**
 
 
• **Photosynthesis:** Converts sunlight into chemical energy stored in glucose molecules.
 
• **Oxygen production:** Releases oxygen as a by-product of photosynthesis, essential for the survival of aerobic organisms.
 
• **Storage:** In some plants, chloroplasts also store starch and other molecules.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Plastids:**
 
 
• **Chromoplasts:** Coloured plastids responsible for the pigment production in fruits and flowers.
 
• **Leucoplasts:** Colourless plastids that store starch, lipids, and proteins in non-photosynthetic tissues.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a part of the fiscal policy of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Monetary Policy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **fiscal policy** refers to the use of government revenue collection (mainly taxes) and expenditure to influence the country's economy. It primarily involves **government spending, taxation, and borrowing.**
 
• **Subsidy**: Subsidies are a key part of fiscal policy. They are financial aids provided by the government to support sectors such as agriculture, education, and healthcare to promote social welfare. *Hence, this is a part of fiscal policy.*
 
• **Welfare Expenditure**: Government spending on welfare schemes like healthcare, education, and poverty alleviation also comes under fiscal policy. These expenses are aimed at improving the socio-economic conditions of the population. *Hence, this is a part of fiscal policy.*
 
• **Investment Strategies**: The government plans and executes investment strategies to foster economic growth and development, which is a key component of fiscal policy. *Hence, this is a part of fiscal policy.*
 
• **Monetary Policy**: Unlike fiscal policy, monetary policy is implemented by the central bank (RBI in India) and involves measures like controlling the money supply, interest rates, and inflation. It is not a part of fiscal policy. *Hence, this is the correct answer.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fiscal Policy:**

 
 
• Formulated by the **Ministry of Finance**, fiscal policy addresses taxation, government spending, and borrowing to influence economic activity.
 
• Its primary objectives include controlling inflation, reducing unemployment, and ensuring equitable distribution of income.
 
• Examples of fiscal tools include **direct taxes (income tax, corporate tax)** and **indirect taxes (GST)**, subsidies, and public debt management.
 
 
 
• **Monetary Policy:**
 
 
• Implemented by the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**, monetary policy aims to regulate the money supply and control inflation and deflation.
 
• Key tools include the **repo rate, reverse repo rate, cash reserve ratio (CRR)**, and **statutory liquidity ratio (SLR)**.
 
• It is categorized into **expansionary policy** (to boost economic activity) and **contractionary policy** (to control inflation).
 
 
 
• **Subsidies:**
 
 
• Subsidies are financial support provided by the government to make goods and services affordable for the population.
 
• Examples include **food subsidies under the Public Distribution System (PDS)**, **fertilizer subsidies** for farmers, and **education subsidies**.
 
 
 
• **Welfare Expenditure:**
 
 
• Includes spending on social welfare schemes such as **healthcare (Ayushman Bharat)**, **education (Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan)**, and rural development schemes like **Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA).**
 
• Aims to reduce poverty, ensure social justice, and promote inclusive growth.
 
 
 
• **Investment Strategies:**
 
 
• Governments invest in infrastructure, technology, and other critical sectors to boost economic growth.
 
• Examples include **Make in India**, **Digital India**, and **Smart Cities Mission**.

questions.question: Which of the following are new fold mountains?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Shivalik Range**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Shivalik Range**, also known as the Outer Himalayas, is classified as a **new fold mountain**. It is the youngest among the Himalayan ranges and is geologically active.
 
• These mountains were formed during the **Tertiary period** (approximately 2-20 million years ago) due to the collision of the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates.
 
• The Shivalik range is characterized by its **steep slopes, river valleys, and sedimentary deposits**. It forms the outermost range of the Himalayas and stretches from Jammu and Kashmir to Arunachal Pradesh.
 
• Unlike the Vindhya, Aravalli, and Satpura ranges, which are older and more stable, the Shivalik Range is still undergoing geological changes due to tectonic activity.
 
• The Shivalik hills serve as a crucial geographical feature in India, separating the plains from the inner Himalayan ranges and influencing the country’s climate and river systems.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Vindhya Range:**

 
 
• This is an older mountain range located in central India, primarily spread across **Madhya Pradesh** and parts of Uttar Pradesh.
 
• The Vindhya range is made up of **sedimentary rocks** and is considered a **block mountain**.
 
• It does not belong to the category of fold mountains and is much older than the Shivalik Range.
 
 
 
• **Aravalli Range:**
 
 
• The Aravalli Range is one of the **oldest fold mountains** in the world, located in **north-western India**, particularly in Rajasthan.
 
• Formed during the **Precambrian era** (approximately 3.2 billion years ago), the Aravallis are geologically stable and heavily eroded.
 
• Unlike the Shivaliks, they are not tectonically active.
 
 
 
• **Satpura Range:**
 
 
• The Satpura Range is located in central India and forms the **southern boundary of the Narmada River** valley.
 
• It is a **block mountain** and is geologically older than the Shivalik Range.
 
• Unlike the Shivaliks, the Satpura range is not categorized as a fold mountain.
 
 
 
• **New Fold Mountains:**
 
 
• New fold mountains, like the Himalayas, are formed due to the tectonic collision of plates and are typically **young, steep, and geologically active**.
 
• The Shivalik Range, being the outermost and youngest part of the Himalayas, falls into this category.
 
• They are characterized by frequent **earthquakes, high peaks, and sharp ridges**.
 
 
 
• [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 
• The **Shivalik Range** is also known for its **Churia Hills** in Nepal and forms a crucial part of the Himalayan ecosystem.
 
• Rivers such as the **Ganga, Yamuna, and Brahmaputra** flow through the Shivaliks, contributing to the fertile Indo-Gangetic plains.
 
• Compared to older mountain ranges like the Vindhyas and Aravallis, the Shivalik range has a **higher rate of erosion** due to its young age.

questions.question: Kashi Vishwanath Temple is situated on the banks of which of the following rivers?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ganges**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Kashi Vishwanath Temple**, located in **Varanasi**, is one of the most famous and sacred Hindu temples dedicated to Lord Shiva.
 
• This iconic temple is situated on the western bank of the **River Ganges**, making it one of the holiest locations for Hindus.
 
• The temple is considered a **Jyotirlinga shrine**, one of the twelve sacred Jyotirlingas of Lord Shiva spread across India.
 
• Varanasi, where the temple is located, is often referred to as the **Spiritual Capital of India** and has been a center of religious and cultural activities for thousands of years.
 
• The **Ganges River**, which flows adjacent to the temple, is revered in Hinduism as a sacred river believed to purify sins and grant salvation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **About the Kashi Vishwanath Temple:**

 
 
• The temple was originally constructed by **Maharani Ahilyabai Holkar** of Indore in the year **1780**.
 
• It is one of the most important pilgrimage sites in India and attracts millions of devotees annually.
 
• The temple is part of the **Kashi Vishwanath Corridor Project**, inaugurated in **2021** to improve infrastructure and facilities for pilgrims.
 
 
 
• **The Ganges River:**
 
 
• The **Ganges River** is the longest river in India, stretching over **2,525 kilometers** and originating from the **Gangotri Glacier** in the Himalayas.
 
• It holds immense religious significance in Hinduism and is considered a goddess named **Ganga Devi**.
 
• Major cities along its course include **Haridwar, Allahabad (Prayagraj), and Varanasi**.
 
• Rituals like **Ganga Aarti** are conducted daily at numerous ghats along the river, including the famous **Dashashwamedh Ghat** in Varanasi.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Jyotirlingas:**
 
 
• Jyotirlingas are considered the most sacred representations of Lord Shiva, manifesting as a column of light.
 
• The Kashi Vishwanath Temple is one of the twelve **Jyotirlingas**, including others like **Somnath** (Gujarat) and **Mahakaleshwar** (Madhya Pradesh).
 
• Visiting Jyotirlingas is believed to bring spiritual liberation and divine blessings.
 
 
 
• **Varanasi as a Spiritual Hub:**
 
 
• Varanasi, also known as **Kashi**, is believed to be one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world.
 
• The city is a center for learning, art, and spirituality, with numerous temples, ghats, and religious institutions.
 
• It is also a significant site for the **Hindu rituals of cremation** and salvation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Penicillium** is a **fungus** that belongs to the phylum **Ascomycota** and is well-known for its ability to produce the antibiotic **penicillin**.
 
• It is a genus of fungi commonly found in soil, decaying organic matter, and indoor environments as a mold species.
 
• **Penicillium** plays a significant role in the medical field for its use in producing antibiotics and also in the food industry, especially in the production of cheeses like **Roquefort** and **Camembert**.
 
• Unlike the other options listed, Penicillium is classified as a fungus due to its specific structural and reproductive characteristics, such as the production of spores.
 
• Other options, such as **Amoeba** (a protozoan) and **Chlamydomonas** or **Spirogyra** (both algae), are not classified as fungi.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Characteristics of Penicillium:**

 
 
• Penicillium is a **saprophytic fungus**, meaning it feeds on decaying organic matter.
 
• It reproduces both sexually and asexually, with asexual reproduction occurring through the formation of **conidia**, which are spore-like structures.
 
• Penicillium species are known for their bluish-green or greenish color on moldy surfaces.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Penicillium:**
 
 
• The antibiotic **penicillin** was first discovered in 1928 by **Alexander Fleming** from the Penicillium notatum mold.
 
• Penicillium species are used in the food industry for the ripening and flavoring of certain cheeses.
 
• Some species of Penicillium produce toxins, such as **mycotoxins**, which can be harmful if ingested.
 
 
 
• **Key Characteristics of Other Options:**
 
 
• **Amoeba:** A unicellular protozoan belonging to the kingdom Protista. It moves and engulfs food using pseudopodia.
 
• **Chlamydomonas:** A unicellular green alga found in freshwater environments. It contains chlorophyll and performs photosynthesis.
 
• **Spirogyra:** A filamentous green alga known for its spiral-shaped chloroplasts, commonly found in freshwater habitats.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• Fungi are eukaryotic organisms that include molds, yeasts, and mushrooms.
 
• They are heterotrophic and can be saprophytic or parasitic in nature.
 
• Unlike algae or protozoa, fungi lack chlorophyll and cannot perform photosynthesis.

questions.question: In which of the following years were elections held for provincial legislatures and ministries throughout British India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1937**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **elections for provincial legislatures and ministries** throughout British India were held in **1937** under the provisions of the **Government of India Act, 1935**.
 
• The **Government of India Act, 1935** introduced provincial autonomy, allowing Indians to control certain aspects of governance in provinces while the British retained control over defense and foreign affairs.
 
• This was the first time that significant powers were handed to Indians in the provinces, and elections were conducted to form **provincial governments**.
 
• The elections were held in **11 provinces**, including Bengal, Punjab, the United Provinces, Bihar, and Bombay.
 
• The **Indian National Congress** performed well in these elections, forming ministries in most provinces, while the **Muslim League** performed poorly, reflecting the limited reach of its mass appeal at that time.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Government of India Act, 1935:**

 
 
• This was the most comprehensive legislation passed by the British Parliament for governing India before independence.
 
• It introduced **provincial autonomy** and separated the responsibilities between the central and provincial governments.
 
• The Act also provided for the establishment of a **bicameral legislature** at the central level and allowed provinces to form their own governments.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of the 1937 Elections:**
 
 
• The elections were the first under the new constitutional reforms introduced by the Government of India Act, 1935.
 
• These elections marked a significant step towards self-governance, as Indians were allowed to govern in certain areas without British interference.
 
• Out of the 11 provinces, Congress won a majority in 8 provinces, including the United Provinces and Bihar.
 
 
 
• **Role of Political Parties:**
 
 
• The **Indian National Congress** emerged as the dominant political force, forming ministries in several provinces and implementing various welfare policies.
 
• The **Muslim League** did not perform well, highlighting its limited influence among Indian Muslims at the time.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the 1937 Elections:**
 
 
• The elections highlighted the growing influence of the Indian National Congress in Indian politics.
 
• They also exposed the weaknesses of the Muslim League, which later contributed to its demand for a separate state (Pakistan).
 
• The elections were a precursor to the political developments leading to India's independence in 1947.
